title: Algorithmic Problem Solving: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (Single & Infinite Transactions)

assessment_targets.what_taught_summary: The stock trading problem involves maximizing profit from an array of daily prices, with specific constraints such as single transaction (buy once, sell once) or infinite transactions (unlimited buy/sell pairs).
assessment_targets.why_assessed_pedagogy: To ensure students can accurately recall the problem definition and constraints before attempting algorithmic solutions.
misconception_distractor_hints: Assuming the trader can hold multiple stocks simultaneously without limit.
Confusing the input array with a time-series graph where interpolation is allowed.
Believing that the goal is to minimize loss rather than maximize profit.

assessment_targets.what_taught_summary: The brute force approach for single transactions requires checking all possible buy-sell pairs to find the maximum difference where the buy index is less than the sell index, resulting in O(n^2) complexity.
assessment_targets.why_assessed_pedagogy: To help students understand the logical baseline of the problem and recognize the inefficiency of exhaustive search before introducing optimizations.
misconception_distractor_hints: Thinking that finding the global minimum and global maximum independently always yields the correct profit.
Assuming that a nested loop is unnecessary because the array is sorted.
Believing that the brute force method can be optimized by simply sorting the array.

assessment_targets.what_taught_summary: The optimized single transaction solution uses a single pass through the array, maintaining a running minimum price and updating the maximum profit whenever the current price exceeds the minimum by more than the current max profit.
assessment_targets.why_assessed_pedagogy: To demonstrate the application of state tracking (min_price, max_profit) to reduce time complexity from O(n^2) to O(n) for the single transaction constraint.
misconception_distractor_hints: Updating min_price after calculating profit instead of before, leading to incorrect comparisons.
Failing to initialize min_price to the first element, causing index errors or incorrect baselines.
Assuming that the maximum profit must occur at the last element of the array.

assessment_targets.what_taught_summary: For infinite transactions, the optimal strategy is to sum all positive differences between consecutive days (prices[i+1] - prices[i]), which is equivalent to capturing every upward movement in the price trend.
assessment_targets.why_assessed_pedagogy: To enable students to analyze the structural difference between single and infinite transaction constraints and derive the greedy algorithm based on local maxima.
misconception_distractor_hints: Attempting to use the single transaction logic (min/max tracking) for infinite transactions.
Believing that one must wait for a global peak to sell, missing intermediate profits.
Subtracting negative differences from the total profit instead of ignoring them.

assessment_targets.what_taught_summary: Dynamic programming generalizes the stock problem by defining states for holding or not holding stock, allowing the formulation of recurrence relations that can handle various transaction limits (k transactions).
assessment_targets.why_assessed_pedagogy: To guide students in analyzing how specific greedy or single-pass solutions are special cases of a broader dynamic programming framework for constrained optimization.
misconception_distractor_hints: Thinking that dynamic programming is only useful for infinite transactions and not for single transactions.
Confusing the state variables (cash, stock) with the price array indices.
Assuming that the DP solution always requires O(n*k) space without considering space optimization.
